name: Stigler's Law of Eponymy
statement: No scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer.
meaning: Discoveries, laws, and theorems are routinely named after someone other than the person who first found them. The eponym rarely marks the true originator.
mechanism: Credit accrues to whoever popularises, systematises, or makes a discovery legible to a community — not the originator, who may have published obscurely, prematurely, or without follow-through. Stigler tied this directly to Merton's Matthew effect: recognition flows to the already-eminent, so an established name becomes the durable label. Naming is a social act of attribution, not a historical audit; the community attaches the name it repeatedly hears.

examples.text: The relation was known to Babylonian mathematicians, and appears in Indian sources, centuries before Pythagoras — who may never have proved it himself.
The normal distribution was first derived by Abraham de Moivre in a 1733 pamphlet, some 76 years before Gauss's 1809 work — yet it carries Gauss's name.

Georges Lemaître published the velocity–distance relation in 1927, two years before Hubble, in a low-circulation French journal. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union voted to rename it the Hubble–Lemaître law.

variants.name: The self-reference
variants.text: Stigler made the law obey itself: he credited its true discovery to the sociologist Robert K. Merton — so a law about misattribution is, by design, misattributed to Stigler.

variants.name: The Matthew effect
variants.text: Merton's engine for the whole phenomenon: eminent scientists get outsized credit, so the famous name sticks and the obscure originator is forgotten.

variants.name: Boyer's law
variants.text: The mathematics-specific version, named by Hubert Kennedy after Carl Boyer: 'mathematical formulas and theorems are usually not named after their original discoverers' — itself a law confirming its own claim.

whyItMatters: It is a standing warning to historians and scientists alike: the name on a law is a clue about who made it famous, not who found it first. It reframes eponymy as a social record of influence rather than a ledger of priority.

working.lead: Don't read priority off the name
working.text: an eponym tells you who popularised a result, not who discovered it; check the actual history before crediting.

working.lead: Expect the namesake to be a systematiser
working.text: the person who made a finding legible and influential usually collects the name, even when someone earlier had it first.
simultaneous and independent discovery is common, so 'the original discoverer' is often genuinely contestable, not just mislabelled.

limits: The 'no discovery' form is deliberately hyperbolic and self-parodying, not literally true — plenty of results are correctly named for their discoverers (Newton's laws, Einstein's relativity, Planck's constant). It is an ironic sociological observation, not a measured or falsifiable regularity; there is no counted rate of misattribution behind it. And 'original discoverer' is itself often ambiguous, since priority disputes and independent discovery muddy who was really first.
misreadings: It is not a claim that scientists routinely steal credit, nor that every eponym is wrong. It observes that fame, not priority, drives naming — a wry point about how communities remember, not an accusation of fraud.
origin: Formulated by the statistician Stephen Stigler in 1980, in a paper titled 'Stigler's Law of Eponymy' published in the Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences and in a festschrift for Robert K. Merton. Stigler credited the law's true discovery to Merton himself — an intentional self-application — and grounded it in Merton's earlier work on the Matthew effect and priority in science.

sources.text: Stigler, S.M. (1980). "Stigler's Law of Eponymy." Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences, 39, 147–157.
